newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVT AGREES TO FORM UNIT TO BUY BANKS' DEBT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVT AGREES TO FORM UNIT TO BUY BANKS' DEBT.

text.p: The Czech government on Wednesday said it had agreed to form a state firm which would buy non-performing credit from the country's smaller banks.
"The basic idea of this plan is the buying of low-quality assets of these banks," Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus told a news conference following a cabinet meeting.
He said that firm, to be called Ceska Financni sro, would be set up for a five to seven year period.

Klaus did not give a specific total of how much the purchase of bad debt was expected to cost the state, but that if all the credit from all the "small domestic banks" would be included in the programme, it would total about 13 billion crowns.
He said the programme would be voluntary and open to all small domestic banks and that the banks would have the option of buying the credit back at a later period.
He said all details would come later from the central bank, the Czech National Bank.

The Czech banking system has been stung by the failure of Plzen-based Kreditni Banka a.s. in August, which became the 11th small or medium-sized bank to be put into forced administration or shut by the central bank in the post-Communist period.
"This proposal...is not some backwards-aimed solution for some concrete bank, but it is an attempt to prevent, in advance, the evolution of problems of this or that bank," Klaus said.

The Czech National Bank has said that the country's four largest banks, which comprise over 70 percent of banking activity, are basically sound and have sufficient reserves to cover their classified credit.
A central bank report to parliament in September blamed the problems of upstart smaller banks on the lending environment surrounding the country's massive post-Communist privatisation programme.
CNB officials were not immediately available to comment on the cabinet's new initiative.
